why: Risk of bias: two domains are high. Participants: two-gate sampling of 12 TEE-proven thrombi and 12 matched controls free of thrombus and SEC, with SEC patients not enrolled. Index test: CT thrombi identified and ROIs placed with knowledge of TEE and with a TEE expert. Target condition (multiplane TEE in all, before CT, within 3 days) and Analysis (24/24 analysed per patient) are low. Applicability: high because of the participant spectrum (selected on TEE, no SEC); index test and target condition are low. This is a proof-of-principle study with continuous values only (Table S6); the reported thrombus versus pectinate-muscle differences are likely larger than would be seen in a consecutive pre-ablation cohort.

High risk of bias in two domains: participants (two-gate design with TEE-positive stroke cases and normal-TEE pre-ablation controls, likely inflating specificity) and index test (iodine cutoff optimised retrospectively in 13 thrombi, likely inflating both sensitivity and specificity). Target condition and analysis are at low risk. High applicability concern from the index test: the iodine values come from a non-gated dual-injection protocol with a 180-s delayed component (120 mL contrast), not from an early-phase or stroke-CTA acquisition. The 100%/100% estimate should be read as optimistic.

Only the index-test domain was re-assessed and it is at low risk for this qualitative reading; participants (high, two-gate), target condition (low) and analysis (low) carry over from E1, so the overall risk of bias is high, mainly through specificity (32/50 includes 31 normal-TEE controls). High applicability concern because the comparator was read on the same non-standard acquisition and the image type is not stated.

Participants and analysis are at low risk for this filling-defect subset, and the target condition (low) carries over from E1; the index-test domain carries over as high (cutoff derived and evaluated in the same 13 thrombi and 18 SEC), so the overall risk of bias is high. Applicability concern is high because of the non-standard dual-injection acquisition with a delayed component (index test, carried over from E1); participants and target condition raise low concern.

Risk high: Domains 3 and 4 are high for one shared reason, selective verification. TEE was done in 19% of the patients who had cardiac PCD-CT, selected by age and by clinical discretion that may have used the CT, and the unverified were excluded without correction; the authors themselves flag selection and verification bias. A CT–TEE interval of up to 21 days, with anticoagulation in between, probably lowered specificity (all 3 false positives at 5 days). Participants and index test are low risk. Applicability: low concern in Domains 1–3 (acute stroke work-up population, photon-counting CT read on polychromatic images as defined for Q4, TEE reference).

Domains 3 and 4 remain high because selective verification is unchanged; Domains 1 and 2 as E1 (low). Limiting the interval to ⩽3 days removes the main timing concern and shows its direction (specificity 96.7% to 100%, sensitivity 90.0% to 88.9%). Applicability as E1 (low concern).

Overall high risk of bias, driven only by the index-test domain: the −1.3 mg/ml cut-off was optimized retrospectively in the same patients (10 thrombi, no validation set), so sensitivity (10/10) and specificity (291/292) are probably optimistic. Participants (prospective consecutive pre-ablation cohort), target condition (multiplane TEE with explicit definitions, < 72 h) and analysis (95.6% of scheduled patients analysed, patient-level 2×2) are low risk. Applicability is of low concern in all three domains. The dual-enhanced single-phase protocol and the platform-specific negative iodine cut-off limit transfer to other scanners and protocols.

Overall high risk: participants, target condition and analysis as for E1 (low); index test high (ROC-optimized 0.304 cut-off with 10 thrombi; HU ratio measured in ROIs guided by the DECT and iodine-map reading rather than by an independent conventional read). Fig. 3 labels a thrombus with a ratio of 0.332 a false negative, whereas Table 1 reports 10/10, so the comparator's 2×2 may contain an error. For the Q2 comparison both tests are fully paired (same acquisition, patients and blinded readers), but both cut-offs were optimized in the same data; QUADAS-C applies. Applicability low.

Overall high risk because the reconstructed operating point (10/10; 26/27) uses the cut-off optimized in these same 37 patients (10 thrombi). Participants low (complete consecutive thrombus and SEC series; selection by TEE category flagged but unlikely to inflate accuracy), target condition low (as E1), analysis low (standard ROC; reconstruction consistent with the AUC and Table 1). If only the threshold-free AUC is synthesized, the index-test domain and the overall judgment would be low. Applicability low in all domains.

Risk of bias is high because the index test domain is high: sensitivity and specificity were computed at a data-driven 'best' cut-off (≤ −0.09) derived in the same data with only 15 thrombus-positive patients. Participants (prospective consecutive pre-ablation AF cohort), target condition (multiplane TEE within 48 h, SEC negative, all analysed patients verified) and analysis (94.9% analysed, patient-level 2×2) are at low risk. Applicability concerns are low in the participants, index test and target condition domains.

High because the index test domain is high (data-driven HU-ratio cut-off, 15 reference-positive patients). Participants, target condition and analysis are unchanged from E1 (low), and applicability is low in all three domains. E1 and E2 share patients, readers and cut-off method, so the spectral-versus-conventional comparison itself is better judged with QUADAS-C.

High risk: the participants domain is high (subset selected on the TEE result, SEC controls mostly mild) and the index test domain is high as in E1 (same data-driven cut-off, probably derived in these 48 patients; the AUC itself is threshold-free but remains affected by the participant selection). Target condition (as E1) and analysis are low. Applicability concern is high because the subgroup is defined by TEE rather than by a filling defect on CT; index test and target condition applicability are low as in E1.

Target condition and Analysis are high risk: only 20 of 50 patients were verified, by TEE or cardiac CTA chosen on clinical grounds; intervals reached 21 days (the only false negative was a thrombus found on a day-21 TEE after new-onset AF); and missing reference data were not handled. Participants and Index test are low risk. Applicability concern is high for the index test: a delayed-phase, non-gated, low-dose chest spectral CT read qualitatively on combined conventional/MonoE/iodine images by one expert, not the early-phase spectral measurement of the ideal trial; participants and target condition raise low concern. The LAA 2×2 (2/1/0/17) was reconstructed by the reviewers because the authors report accuracy only for any cardioembolic source, and it rests on 3 reference-positive patients.

High risk in Target condition and Analysis for the same reasons as E1, plus verification and reference assessment that were not independent of the conventional images and a 2×2 with one unresolved cell (specificity 16/17 or 17/17). Index test is low risk, but reader expertise differed between the conventional and spectral readings. Applicability concern is high because the comparator is the conventional reading of a delayed-phase, non-gated, low-dose chest scan. Sensitivity rests on 3 reference-positive patients (1/3).

Overall high risk of bias, driven by the index-test domain: the iodine cut-off of ≤ 8.9 mg/cm³ (and the alternative ≤ 2.3 mg/cm³) was derived post hoc in the same 26 patients to reach 100% sensitivity (or specificity) with only 6 TEE-positive patients, so the estimate is optimistic. Participants (single-gate, prospective; selected but not enriched), target condition (blinded multiplane TEE in all, median interval 0 days) and analysis (6/32 not in the spectral 2×2 because of protocol assignment, all TEE-negative) are low risk. Applicability is low in all three domains (TEE-referred outpatients mostly in AF; dual-source dual-energy iodine quantification on a single dual-enhancement acquisition; TEE-defined thrombus). Main limitations for the synthesis: data-driven threshold, very few positives, no reported CIs, and a flow diagram inconsistent with the tables (20 vs 26 dual-energy scans).

Overall low risk: visual reading by a blinded reader without a threshold (index-test domain low), with participants, target condition and analysis as for E1 (all low). Applicability low; whether blended images alone were used for the visual reading is not stated. For the paired comparison with E1, only the spectral arm had an optimised cut-off, which favours iodine concentration (a QUADAS-C issue).

Risk: participants low, index test high, target condition low, analysis low; one high domain makes the overall judgment high. The 100% specificity depends on an undefined, not pre-specified iodine rule applied without reported blinding to the 7 equivocal phase-III cases, in a study with 14 thrombi. Applicability: participants low, index test high, target condition low. The spectral parameter was measured only on the 3.5-min delayed phase and decided only 21 patients after three conditional delayed scans, so the 2x2 mostly reflects conventional delayed imaging.

Risk: index test low; participants, target condition and analysis carried over from E1, all low. Applicability low in all three domains (participants and target condition from E1). For the Q2 comparison, E1 is nested in E2 (iodine read only in E2-positive patients) and is itself at high risk with high applicability concern; QUADAS-C would flag the comparison as non-independent.

Risk: participants low, index test high, target condition low (from E1), analysis low. The derived 14/0/0/7 table rests entirely on the undefined iodine rule with no reported blinding. Applicability: participants high (21 patients whose defect persisted after three delayed scans; thrombus prevalence 67%), index test high (delayed phase III), target condition low (from E1; SEC not reported on TEE, so the negatives are all non-thrombus defects).

All four domains at high risk: study group restricted to arterial-phase filling defects (D1); Youden cut-off with 18 reference positives and IC chosen post hoc as the best of five parameters (D2); composite reference that incorporates the same CT examination (9/18 thrombi defined on the 3-min delayed phase), with TEE or surgery for only 7/18 positives and partial and differential verification (D3); only 66/296 filling-defect patients (66/1,459 scanned) analysed, with operating points not reproducible from Fig. 3 (D4). Applicability concern high for the all-patient question because participants and measurement were restricted to filling defects; the target condition matches.

Inherits high risk in participants, target condition and analysis from E1; the comparator itself also rests on a Youden cut-off (45.98 HU) with 18 reference positives. Both tests were measured in the same patients and ROIs with the same reference, so the paired comparison is internally consistent, but every estimate is at high risk. Applicability concern high as for E1.

Participants suit the filling-defect question (D1 low), but risk stays high for the index test (Youden cut-off, 18 positives, post hoc parameter choice), the target condition (incorporation of the same CT examination, composite reference with partial and differential verification) and the analysis (66/296 analysed, operating points not reproducible from Fig. 3). Applicability concern low: participants, test and target condition match Q3.
